 Taiwan shuts down ahead of Typhoon Champi, hundreds of flights cancelled 
 PUBLISHED : 23 Oct 2026 at 10:44
 WRITER: 
 Reuters 
 Listen 
   Small 
   Medium 
   Large 
 Share
 Facebook
 Reddit
 Copy Link
 A boat travels near a breakwater as waves generated by Typhoon Champi hit Badouzi Fishing Port in Keelung, Taiwan, on Friday. (Photo: Reuters) 
 YILAN, Taiwan - Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, and though the storm is weakening it could still make direct landfall on the island.
 At one point a super typhoon and one of the ​strongest storms in the Pacific this ⁠year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kilometres per hour near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA).
 The storm was about 320km east of Taiwan's southern tip, the CWA said. The storm's forecast track ‌shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north towards the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan.
 One person was killed and 94 were injured in Taiwan, where the government said almost 1,300 people had been evacuated from mountainous areas.
 CWA forecaster Liu ⁠Pei-teng told Reuters that landfall could not be ruled out if it "stalls, loops, or wobbles from side to side" on approach to Taiwan.
 "The storm's wind radius is quite large, among the bigger ones in recent years," Liu said. "If the storm slows down, the strong winds will affect Taiwan for longer."
 Coastal towns received mobile phone alerts warning of gusts exceeding 150kph and urging residents ​to seek immediate shelter, while nearly a metre of rain was forecast for northern mountain areas, including around Taipei.
 In the northeastern county of Yilan, where strong winds and heavy showers were intensifying ​and ‌the typhoon was forecast to pass close by later on Friday, authorities distributed sandbags and put amphibious vehicles and inflatable rescue boats on standby.
 "When necessary, the military will come in to help people, including ​using ⁠amphibious vehicles for evacuations or disaster relief," said Lee Ming-chen, head of the port town of Suao, which was badly flooded in previous typhoons.
 Huge radius 
 Taiwan forecasters said the storm's ⁠radius was around 320km, large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days.
 Taiwan's financial markets also closed on Friday, while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices ⁠as normal.
 The Transport Ministry said all 262 domestic flights were cancelled for Friday, along with 669 international ​ones. The north-south high-speed rail service was operating as usual.
 In the capital Taipei there were squally showers, but public transport including the subway was working, albeit with reduced service.
 Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can ‌strike in autumn too.
 The typhoon ⁠is forecast to first pass over Japan's westernmost inhabited ​island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa prefecture.
